parts.title: Why Does the Fridge Door STAY Shut? Magnets Hiding at Home (Part 1) | Magnets in Everyday Life
parts.description:
Pip pushes his fridge door and it swings shut by itself, with no lock and no catch. What keeps it closed? Lock in your answer from last time, be the magnetic strip inside the door, look inside the fridge door's soft edge, spot Basil's shiny mistake, and find the steel hiding in a whiteboard and a doorstop. Part 1 of Primary 3 Science, Making and Using Magnets: magnets in everyday life.

In this part:
• What keeps the fridge door closed? (last episode's dare)
• Be the magnetic strip
• Look closer: the fridge door's soft edge
• HOLD ON! Is a shiny window frame magnetic?
• Look closer: a whiteboard and a doorstop
• Spot the hidden honeybee!

Key words: magnetic strip, magnetic whiteboard, magnetic doorstop.
Watch Part 2: cranes, floating trains, the MRI scanner and a magnet toy. Last episode: was that test fair?

TheOneApp, Explained: Singapore primary science, made fun. Play along with Pip, Basil and Momo: show fingers to lock in, keep score on your hand, beat the Buddies!

Where do magnets hide in everyday life? P3 Science, Chapter 7, Making and Using Magnets (pp. 119 to 126): Strips of magnets can be found inside the doors of a refrigerator. These help to keep the door closed. The crane has a large iron disc that becomes a powerful electromagnet. The electromagnet then attracts objects made of iron and steel. Some whiteboards have steel sheets under the writing surfaces. These allow magnets to be attracted to the whiteboards. The magnet on a doorstop helps to hold the door in place and prevents it from closing suddenly. The magnets on the train and the tracks repel one another. MRI is a safe and painless test. Properties of magnets allow us to use magnets in everyday life. The last episode of the Magnets theme and of Primary 3. Also fits US NGSS 3-PS2-4 (Grade 3 design challenge with magnets).
Safety and care: Keep small magnets away from your mouth and from little brothers and sisters. Scrapyards are for workers only: we watch from outside. We look at honeybees and water striders, and we do not touch them.
Try it at home: count the magnets in your home today, and tell someone how many you found. Then design a magnet toy: which poles will face each other, and why?
Pip's HDB flat, a Family Day at a park pond in Singapore, a scrapyard in Singapore or in the US.

parts.title: A Train That FLOATS? Cranes, Trains and a Magnet Toy (Part 2) | Magnets in Everyday Life

• Magnets interacting
• A chant to remember it all
